Atlas 0.1 · PoC 4 · coupled episode

A rocket, marched

Six compressible gas blocks, a two-panel conducting airframe and a 3-DOF rigid body, advanced together for 0.145 s of flight at 25 km and Mach 3.5. Re-marched four times. The seams were rebuilt first: blocks that share a seam now share its node lines, and the coupler exchanges across each one by position, in each block's own gas model. That run failed its symmetry checks. The cause was a wall in the gas solver that passed mass, and the second re-march fixed it. An audit of that run for conservation then found four more defects in the code: an injector that delivered 17.7% more mass than it declared, a throat seam that lost 3% of the mass flow every step, stationary walls that did work, and a skin that radiated to the air beside it instead of to the sky. The third re-march fixed all four. This is the fourth: it also couples the seam between the air ahead of the vehicle and the wake behind it both ways, where the wake had only been reading the air.

The vehicle

Every block in SI units on one scale per field, so a seam shows a jump only where the physics has one. The domain is 8.0 m long and the engine is 0.70 m of it, so there are two views: the whole field, and the engine at about four times the linear scale. The nose is at the left, at z = −4 m; the exhaust leaves to the right. The strip ahead of the nose is the forebody slot, a region the configuration declares unmodelled: the air passes it along a slip, adiabatic wall, and nothing there counts as vehicle.

The airframe

The skin is 8 mm thick and 4.7 m long, in two panels either side of the axis, conducting along its length and loaded by the gas on both faces. Over the tank barrel (z < 0) the inner face borders a region no block models, and sees the wall the configuration declares there: adiabatic, at ambient pressure. Nose at the left.

Skin temperatureK
Von Mises stressMPa
Transverse displacementmm, lower panel negated

The third plot is the check on the panels: a symmetric vehicle at zero incidence bends its two panels as mirror images, so the upper panel's displacement and the lower panel's, negated, should be one line. In the first march they were the same line un-negated — the lower panel was loaded inside out, by up to 4.17 m on a body 0.22 m wide.

Drag and side forceN/m

Planar model: forces are per metre of depth, and so is the 50 t mass the rigid body carries. Drag is the aerodynamic force along the body axis towards the tail — pressure and wall shear over both panels of the atmosphere block — and the side force is what a symmetric body at zero incidence must not have.

The macro step is a declaration

This ran at Δtmacro = 5×10−3 s against the configuration's own 5×10−2. A tenfold reduction, and a conservative one: one chamber flow-through is about 6×10−3 s, so this sits at 0.83 flow-throughs. The multirate lag defect is first order in the exchange interval all the way to the configuration's own step, and the CS-11 bound holds there too, 2.28× loose. So the reduction cuts the coupling defect tenfold; it does not rescue a bound. (Tier 80 had the bound violated at 5×10−2 s, and Tier 84 found a knee at 1.67 flow-throughs. Both were the old isothermal wall's, and both went away when W334 re-derived them with the wall fixed.) What the step costs here: run at 10, 5 and 2.5 ms, the velocity the vehicle gains by 60 ms is 0.534, 0.580 and 0.585 m/s, so this page's 5 ms step sits 0.8% below the extrapolated value. Before the fixes it sat 8% below; most of that was the start-up swing of an over-delivering injector and a leaking throat. Every seam inside the engine now shrinks with the step, as a coupling lag should.

What these numbers can be trusted for

This run was re-run under a ledger that reads the face fluxes the solver itself applies, block by block and seam by seam (W336). Exact: every block conserves mass, momentum and energy to 10−13; the walls pass no mass; the skin's energy balance closes; the injector delivers exactly the declared mass flow; the skin radiates to the ambient; and the re-run reproduces this page's run bitwise. Right to a fraction of a percent: the mass flow through the injector, the throat and the exit agree to 0.1%, and the vehicle loses mass at the rate the nozzle expels it; the chamber runs at 0.98 of its declared 8 MPa; the throat seam creates 3×10−4 of the mass flow late in the run, where it lost 3% (W340: the seam's ghost is now two cell layers deep); the gas's heat loss at the engine walls reaches the skin to 2×10−4, where 4.7% was lost to work at walls that do not move (W339); and the two routes to the thrust agree to 2.5×10−4. Right to about 1%: given its inflow, the nozzle's thrust is 0.992 of ideal planar-nozzle theory. Wrong, with a named cause: the plume's seams do not conserve, because the plume block runs one gas model for exhaust and air (W341); and the seam between the air block and the wake block still loses 1.1% of its mass flow beside the plume, where the wake is subsonic and the two blocks' cells do not line up (W343). Coupling that seam both ways halved the loss from 2.1%. What remains is the same at a 5 ms and a 2.5 ms coupling step, so it is a property of the mismatched grids, not of the lag. Not known at this grid: every wall flux. The engine's wall heat doubles each time the wall cell halves, and at this resolution the air still heats the skin in the wrong direction (W342). The skin temperatures and the drag shown here are not converged. So this is a correct demonstration of the coupled machinery at its declared operating point, and not yet a quantitative prediction of the vehicle's heating or drag.
